jenna_support: Hey @lina_customer — saw you opened a ticket about requests to our inference endpoint failing from your VPC. Can you confirm it's all requests or just long-running streams?

lina_customer: All requests. Short ones sometimes get through, but anything >10s hits TLS handshake errors or ECONNRESET. Happening across multiple hosts in our private subnet.

jenna_support: Thanks. Can you paste one of the client-side error snippets? Any tcpdump or curl output helps.

lina_customer: Sure — curl to our private endpoint (hosted by Redwood Private):
```
curl -v https://private-infer.example.local/predict
* Connected to private-infer.example.local (10.0.5.22) port 443 (#0)
* TLS 1.2 connection using TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
* handshake failed: error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure
* Closing connection 0
curl: (35) error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:sslv3 alert handshake failure
```

ravi_infra: That alert suggests the TLS server is seeing a problem during handshake — could be SNI mismatch or source IP SNAT mapping to a different EIP not on the allowlist. Lina, do you have an egress NAT gateway or NAT instance?

lina_customer: We use a managed NAT gateway in the public subnet. All outbound 0.0.0.0/0 is through that. We did recently rotate NAT EIPs for cost reasons.

aaron_oncall: Quick check: are you using a security appliance (DPI/SSL-inspect) in front of the NAT? Those can terminate TLS and cause handshake alerts.

lina_customer: No DPI. We do have a per-account egress allowlist at Redwood for private deployments — we added the new NAT EIP to the allowlist, but maybe something else changed.

jenna_support: Can you share an instance tcpdump showing the 3-way TCP handshake and then the TLS ClientHello/ServerHello? Even a 10-line extract is useful.

lina_customer: Attached small extract:
```
10:12:01.123 IP 10.0.5.100.52742 > 10.0.5.22.443: Flags [S], seq 0
10:12:01.124 IP 10.0.5.22.443 > 10.0.5.100.52742: Flags [S.], seq 0, ack 1
10:12:01.124 IP 10.0.5.100.52742 > 10.0.5.22.443: Flags [.], ack 1
10:12:01.130 IP 10.0.5.100.52742 > 10.0.5.22.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:513, ack 1, length 512  # ClientHello fragments
10:12:01.131 IP 10.0.5.22.443 > 10.0.5.100.52742: Flags [R], seq 0, ack 1  # immediate RST after ClientHello
```

ravi_infra: Immediate RST after ClientHello on server IP — that implies the server-side process (Redwood Private runtime) or a middlebox is dropping/closing. Are you hitting the endpoint LB IP directly or a private hostname that resolves to a load balancer?

lina_customer: Host resolves to the local control-plane VIP in our VPC: 10.0.5.22 is the inference service's private address (traefik+envoy in front).

aaron_oncall: Two quick hypotheses: 1) The NACL has a stateless deny that blocks ephemeral high ports on the return path causing the server to RST, 2) Source SNAT EIP mismatch on Redwood allowlist so the server-side guard rejects and closes — but reject with RST seems odd.

jenna_support: Can you run `sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v` and `aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=vpc-xxxx` and paste relevant sections? Also confirm ephemeral port range on your hosts: `cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range`.

lina_customer: ip_local_port_range: 32768 60999. NACLs: we have an explicit deny rule for ephemeral outbound ports 60000-61000 (legacy rule) — probably an oversight when we shrank the port space. iptables SNAT shows NAT to EIP 3.101.55.10.

ravi_infra: That matches pattern — your client source ports are in 52742 which is below 60000, so not impacted by that NACL rule. But the server returned RST; could the server be trying to open a connection back to the client on an ephemeral port outside allowed range (for some control channel)? Unlikely for TLS.

aaron_oncall: Another thing: are there asymmetric routes or multiple NAT gateways with different EIPs? If SYN arrives via NAT A (EIP X) and return attempt is routed via NAT B (EIP Y) and only X is allowlisted on Redwood’s side, the server may accept then immediately RST when it fails an auth check tied to source EIP. Lina, you said you rotated NAT EIPs earlier — can you list current NATs and their EIPs and check CloudTrail for SNAT mapping around 10:12:01?

lina_customer: We found two NAT gateways in the route table: nat-0a1 and nat-0b2. nat-0a1 has EIP 3.101.55.10 (we added to Redwood allowlist). nat-0b2 has EIP 54.12.33.77 (forgot to add). Instances in subnet A prefer nat-0a1 but failover can route to nat-0b2 during maintenance windows. The failing host did a failover at 10:11:59 per CloudTrail.

jenna_support: That explains it. When your source IP was 54.12.33.77 (not on our allowlist), our ingress guard likely rejected the TLS session mid-handshake and closed the socket — resulting in the RST you saw. Two action items: 1) Add 54.12.33.77 to your Redwood private egress allowlist, 2) remove the stray/unused NAT gateway or make sure route tables bind to the intended NAT to avoid split brain.

lina_customer: Adding the EIP now. Quick test after adding...

deploy-bot: [system] Updated allowlist entry created for client EIP 54.12.33.77 by jenna_support at 10:40 UTC.

lina_customer: Re-tested — long requests now succeed, no more TLS handshake failures. Thank you! :tada:

ravi_infra: Nice. For prevention, consider enforcing a single NAT with autoscaling or using NAT gateway per AZ with deterministic sticky routing and reflect those EIPs in the allowlist as part of your runbook. Also consider reducing ephemeral port range holes (you have an odd deny 60000-61000) — looks like leftover.

jenna_support: Filing follow-up ticket to update our onboarding doc for Private customers to remind them to sync all NAT EIPs after rotations. Closing this thread if no further issues. :white_check_mark:
